title: Process & Operation Costing
outcomes: Prepare process accounts with normal and abnormal losses or gains.
Compute equivalent production under FIFO and weighted average.
Explain inter-process profit and operation costing.

meta.exam_tip: Always build the units reconciliation first (input = output + losses + closing WIP) before any rupee figure.

concepts.title: Features of process costing and the process account
body: Process costing suits continuous, mass production of identical units passing through sequential processes — chemicals, textiles, paper, oil refining, food processing. Costs are collected per process for a period and averaged over output.

Each process account is debited with materials, labour, direct expenses and overheads, and with the cost of units transferred from the previous process; it is credited with normal loss scrap, abnormal loss and output transferred to the next process or finished stock.
Unlike job costing, costs are not traced to individual orders; work-in-progress is common at period ends and must be converted into equivalent finished units.
concepts.analogy: Costs follow the product through each stage, like water flowing through connected tanks.
concepts.work: A paper mill has pulping, forming and finishing processes, each with its own account.

concepts.title: Normal loss, abnormal loss and abnormal gain
body: Normal loss is the expected, unavoidable loss (evaporation, shrinkage). Its cost is absorbed by good output; scrap value of normal loss is credited to the process.

Abnormal loss is loss beyond normal, from inefficiency or accident. It is valued at the same cost per unit as good output — (total cost − normal scrap) ÷ (input − normal loss) — and credited to the process and debited to an Abnormal Loss Account, which in turn is credited with its scrap value and the balance written off to Costing P&L.

Abnormal gain arises when actual loss is less than normal. It is debited to the process at the normal cost per unit and credited to an Abnormal Gain Account; that account is debited with the scrap value forgone and the balance credited to Costing P&L.
concepts.analogy: Expected losses raise unit cost; unexpected ones are isolated and reported.
concepts.work: Normal loss 5%, actual loss 3%: the 2% difference is an abnormal gain.

concepts.title: Equivalent production: FIFO and weighted average
body: Equivalent units express partly completed units as whole units: units × percentage complete, computed separately for each cost element because materials often enter at the start while conversion accrues gradually.

FIFO: opening WIP is completed first; current-period cost per EU uses only current costs and current work (opening WIP's remaining work + units started and completed + closing WIP work). Opening WIP cost is added only to completed units.
Weighted average: opening WIP cost and current cost are pooled; EU = completed units + closing WIP work; one average rate values both completed units and closing WIP.
Losses in EU: normal loss gets zero EU (its cost spreads to good units); abnormal loss gets EU to the stage of loss, usually 100%.
concepts.analogy: Half-done units are counted as fractions of whole ones so costs can be shared fairly.
concepts.work: 1,000 units 50% converted equal 500 equivalent units of conversion work.

concepts.title: Inter-process profit and operation costing
body: Inter-process profit: when output is transferred between processes at market price or cost plus a percentage, process accounts show profit at each stage. Unrealised profit in closing stock must be eliminated through a provision so that final profit is not overstated.
Operation costing is a refinement of process costing used where each operation is costed (cost per operation), such as in engineering units or bottle filling; it aids control at each step.
Process costing contrasts with job costing: continuous vs. order-based; average costs vs. specific costs; period accumulation vs. job completion.
concepts.analogy: Transfer profits motivate managers but must be removed from unsold stock before reporting.
concepts.work: Process I transfers at cost + 25%; profit on goods still in Process II stock is unrealised.

illustrations.title: A process with losses
illustrations.q: 10,000 units were put into Process I at a total cost of ₹3,02,000 (materials, labour and overheads). Normal loss is 10% of input; loss units sell as scrap at ₹5 each. Actual output was 8,800 units. Prepare the Process I account and value the abnormal loss.

solution.text: Cost per unit = (total cost − scrap of normal loss) ÷ normal output = 2,97,000 ÷ 9,000 = ₹33. The abnormal loss account is then credited with ₹1,000 scrap value and the balance ₹5,600 goes to Costing P&L.

illustrations.title: Finishing what was started last month
illustrations.q: Opening WIP 2,000 units (materials 100%, conversion 60%) valued at ₹70,000. Units introduced 18,000; completed and transferred 17,000; closing WIP 3,000 (materials 100%, conversion 40%). Current costs: materials ₹3,60,000; conversion ₹5,10,000. Using FIFO, compute equivalent units, cost per EU, cost of completed units and closing WIP.

jobs.title: Yield monitoring
jobs.situation: A chemicals plant's losses have crept above the normal rate.
steps: Compare with actual loss to find abnormal loss.
Value it at the process cost per unit.
Report causes and cost to production management.
jobs.takeaway: Separating abnormal loss puts a rupee value on inefficiency.

mcqs.explain: Process costing averages costs over homogeneous output. In practice: refineries and textile mills use it.
mcqs.topic: Features of process costing and the process account

mcqs.q: Scrap value of normal loss is:
mcqs.explain: It reduces the cost borne by good output. In practice: it is a recovery, not income.
mcqs.topic: Normal loss, abnormal loss and abnormal gain

mcqs.q: Input 5,000 units costing ₹1,00,000; normal loss 10% (scrap nil); output 4,400. Abnormal loss value:
mcqs.explain: Cost per unit = 1,00,000 ÷ 4,500 = ₹22.22; abnormal loss 100 units = ₹2,222. In practice: round consistently.
mcqs.topic: Normal loss, abnormal loss and abnormal gain

options: Actual loss is less than normal loss
mcqs.explain: Fewer units lost than expected gives an abnormal gain. In practice: it is credited, net of scrap forgone, to Costing P&L.
mcqs.topic: Normal loss, abnormal loss and abnormal gain

mcqs.q: Under FIFO, cost per EU is based on:
options: Current-period costs and current work only
Opening WIP cost plus current cost
mcqs.explain: FIFO separates opening WIP; weighted average pools. In practice: FIFO gives current efficiency.
mcqs.topic: Equivalent production: FIFO and weighted average

mcqs.q: 2,000 units in closing WIP are 30% complete for conversion. Conversion EU:
mcqs.explain: 2,000 × 30% = 600. In practice: materials may be 100% complete.
mcqs.topic: Equivalent production: FIFO and weighted average

mcqs.q: Normal loss is given equivalent units of:
mcqs.explain: Its cost is absorbed by good units, so no EU is assigned. In practice: abnormal loss gets EU.
mcqs.topic: Equivalent production: FIFO and weighted average

mcqs.q: Unrealised inter-process profit in closing stock is:
mcqs.explain: Only profit on goods sold outside is realised. In practice: compute the profit element in each stock layer.

questions.q: 10,000 units were put into Process I at a total cost of ₹3,02,000 (materials, labour and overheads). Normal loss is 10% of input; loss units sell as scrap at ₹5 each. Actual output was 8,800 units. Prepare the Process I account and value the abnormal loss.

model.text: Cost per unit = (total cost − scrap of normal loss) ÷ normal output = 2,97,000 ÷ 9,000 = ₹33. The abnormal loss account is then credited with ₹1,000 scrap value and the balance ₹5,600 goes to Costing P&L.

questions.q: Opening WIP 2,000 units (materials 100%, conversion 60%) valued at ₹70,000. Units introduced 18,000; completed and transferred 17,000; closing WIP 3,000 (materials 100%, conversion 40%). Current costs: materials ₹3,60,000; conversion ₹5,10,000. Using FIFO, compute equivalent units, cost per EU, cost of completed units and closing WIP.
mistakes: Using weighted average when FIFO is asked.

summary: Process A/c: debit costs; credit normal scrap, abnormal loss, output.
Cost per unit = (cost − normal scrap) ÷ normal output.
Abnormal loss/gain valued at that rate; net to Costing P&L.
EU: FIFO (current only) vs weighted average (pooled).
traps: Abnormal gain account is debited with scrap value forgone.

viva.model: The expected and unavoidable loss inherent in a process, whose cost is absorbed by good output after crediting scrap value.
At the cost per unit of normal output: total cost less scrap of normal loss, divided by input less normal loss units.
A notional whole unit representing partly completed work, found by multiplying units by their percentage of completion.

viva.q: How do FIFO and weighted average differ?
viva.model: FIFO uses only current costs and work and keeps opening WIP separate; weighted average pools opening and current costs into one rate.
A form of process costing that determines the cost of each operation rather than each process, for closer control.

cases.title: PureJuice
cases.case: PureJuice puts 20,000 litres into its pressing process at a cost of ₹4,00,000. Normal loss is 5% (sold as pulp at ₹2 per litre). Output is 19,400 litres.

mcqs.explain: 5% of 20,000 = 1,000. In practice: computed on input.
mcqs.topic: Normal loss, abnormal loss and abnormal gain

mcqs.explain: Expected output 19,000; actual 19,400 — gain 400. In practice: loss was only 600.
mcqs.topic: Normal loss, abnormal loss and abnormal gain

mcqs.q: Cost per litre of normal output:
mcqs.explain: (4,00,000 − 2,000) ÷ 19,000 = ₹20.95 (rounded). In practice: value the gain at this rate.
mcqs.topic: Normal loss, abnormal loss and abnormal gain

mcqs.q: Net abnormal gain credited to Costing P&L:
mcqs.explain: Gain 400 × 20.95 = 8,380 less pulp value forgone 400 × 2 = 800 → ₹7,580. In practice: show it in the abnormal gain account.
mcqs.topic: Normal loss, abnormal loss and abnormal gain
